title: VA's REACH VET suicide-risk model is associated with fewer documented suicide attempts, admissions and ED visits among top-0.1%-risk veterans; no change in mortality
summary: VA-authored triple-difference cohort study (173,313 veterans): REACH VET inclusion linked to more completed visits and safety plans and fewer admissions, ED visits and attempts; no mortality effect.
account: The Department of Veterans Affairs announced on 3 April 2017 that REACH VET (Recovery Engagement and Coordination for Health - Veterans Enhanced Treatment), which uses a predictive model on veterans' health records to identify those at statistically elevated risk of suicide and other adverse outcomes, had begun as a pilot the previous October and was fully implemented across VA; once a veteran is identified, a VA mental health or primary care provider reaches out, reviews the veteran's condition and treatment plan and decides whether enhanced care is needed. Nextgov/FCW (17 July 2025) reports that the model scans records monthly for the top 0.1% risk tier, that the variable set was cut from 381 to 61, and that about 30,000 veterans were identified in the first year; Nextgov (18 October 2024) gives about 6,700 veterans a month. McCarthy and colleagues of the VA Office of Mental Health and Suicide Prevention, which built and runs the program, published the evaluation in JAMA Network Open on 18 October 2021: among 173,313 individuals, including 40,816 in the top 0.1% tier during REACH VET (March 2017 to December 2018) and 36,604 in the pre-period (March 2014 to December 2015), triple-difference analyzes found REACH VET associated with more completed outpatient appointments (adjusted triple difference 0.31; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.55), a higher proportion with new safety plans (0.08; 0.06 to 0.10), and fewer mental health admissions (-0.08; -0.10 to -0.05), emergency department visits (-0.03; -0.06 to -0.01) and documented suicide attempts (-0.05; -0.06 to -0.03); subcohort analyzes found no difference in suicide or all-cause mortality. Care evaluations of identified veterans rose from 46.1% to 87.5% over the period, and a 2022 Psychiatric Services paper reports that by October 2020, 98% of veterans identified (N=6,579) were contacted and had their care evaluated. Dent, Cooper and McCarthy (JAMA Network Open, 8 July 2025; 266,246 observations) again found no association with suicide, external-cause or all-cause mortality (6-month suicide HR 1.18; 95% CI 0.83–1.69). Nextgov (2024) reports research finding the model “considered being a white man more of an indicator of potential self-harm than other factors” and omitted military sexual trauma, and that a REACH VET 2.0 adding such factors was planned for early 2025. The date observed is the publication date of the 2021 evaluation; the program's benefit is a cohort-level association over 2017–2018, not a dated event.
purpose: Built to identify veterans in the top 0.1% of predicted suicide risk each month so that clinicians re-evaluate and enhance their care; the measured associations are that purpose.
system: REACH VET (Recovery Engagement and Coordination for Health - Veterans Enhanced Treatment) suicide-risk predictive model and care-enhancement program
model_version: Original 2017 model (381 variables reduced to 61, per Nextgov); REACH VET 2.0 announced for 2025
developer: US Department of Veterans Affairs, Office of Mental Health and Suicide Prevention
segment: Health-system predictive risk modeling and outreach
taxonomy_note: Loose fit; the outcomes are mental-health care results (fewer attempts, admissions and ED visits) with no effect on deaths, from a VA-authored cohort study.

ratings.reason: The 2021 study reports population-level reductions in documented suicide attempts, admissions and ED visits for identified veterans; no individual veteran's outcome is documented, and mortality did not differ in 2021 or 2025.
Care evaluations rose from 46.1% to 87.5% of identified veterans and 98% were contacted by October 2020, per VA-authored papers; no independent audit was found.
Nextgov notes the top 0.1% tier covers only 2–3% of VA suicides and the model under-identified women; no population suicide-rate effect is shown.

ai_role.statement: The predictive model selects the monthly top 0.1% risk tier; coordinators and providers then re-evaluate care and reach out, so the clinical response, not the model alone, produces any change. The evaluation is observational, uses a triple-difference design to handle non-parallel trends, and is authored by the VA office that built and runs REACH VET; it found no mortality association, replicated in 2025 by the same group, and independent reporting documents that the original model weighted being a white man heavily and omitted military sexual trauma.

produced_by: A predictive model run monthly on VHA electronic health records to rank patients and select the top 0.1% risk tier
Facility REACH VET coordinators and providers who acknowledge the list, evaluate care, document safety plans and attempt outreach
A national health system with the data, dashboards and metrics to implement the program at every facility
must_hold: Providers act on the list: care evaluations rose from 46.1% to 87.5% of identified veterans between March 2017 and December 2018
The model's variables fit the population; the original model under-weighted factors relevant to women veterans, per Nextgov
Outcome ascertainment is comparable across periods; the authors note that closer attention may increase recorded attempts

echoes.setting: VA-authored cohort study of 266,246 observations testing suicide, external-cause and all-cause mortality after REACH VET inclusion; found no association at 6, 12 or 24 months (a different endpoint from the 2021 benefit)
echoes.source: Dent KR, Cooper S, McCarthy JF (2025) JAMA Netw Open, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12238888/

echoes.setting: REACH VET 2.0 adding military sexual trauma and intimate partner violence as risk factors, planned for early 2025 deployment per Nextgov (date is the start of the planned window); no outcome reported

headline: REACH VET tied to fewer suicide attempts, not deaths

comparator.against: veterans in the top 0.1% risk tier during the pre-REACH VET period (March 2014 to December 2015) and subthreshold-risk cohorts, in a triple-difference design
comparator.quote: The REACH VET intervention was associated with significant increases in completed outpatient appointments (adjusted triple difference [ATD], 0.31; 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.55) and proportion of individuals with new safety plans (ATD, 0.08; 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.10) and reductions in mental health admissions (ATD, −0.08; 95% CI, −0.10 to −0.05), emergency department visits (ADT, −0.03; 95% CI, −0.06 to −0.01), and suicide attempts (ADT, −0.05; 95% CI, −0.06 to −0.03).

later.note: Nextgov reported in July 2025 that REACH VET still scans records monthly with the 61-variable model and that VA is updating it to a 2.0 model; a VA cohort study published 8 July 2025 found no association between REACH VET inclusion and suicide or all-cause mortality, in line with the 2021 evaluation's mortality subanalyses.
later.quote: Each month, REACH VET uses the 61 variables to scan the electronic health records of veterans engaged with the Veterans Health Administration to identify those who are in the top 0.1% of suicide risk.
